en: The *Péngzhézhēn* (Needle for Broken Thatch) says: "One who practices virtue while concealing their brilliance may be lofty but remains nameless; one with meager virtue who adapts to the times may be famous but not lofty.

In our own school, there was the Iron Old Man (*Tiěwēng*), who claimed his learning was substantial and desired to have his fame celebrated by posterity. Yet, he was neither truly lofty nor possessed a distinguished reputation.
It would not be improper to use the analogy of the birds and mice. As for Yang Chiyou, I have heard that he was also versed in the Vinaya before I was;
furthermore, my natural disposition has been to critique heterodox views and to criticize predecessors—a trait for which I was disliked by my former teacher.
He often remarked that [Yang] was frivolous and spoke without restraint. Although I knew his innate character was such, I thought his quality lay in his diligence.
He was made to study and learn it; what a pity that, having never experienced the distant transmission, he suddenly gave rise to lax habits and lacked any orthodox lineage.
Relying solely on his own mind, he recklessly engaged in forced interpretations, thereby destroying the ancestral teachings while acting as if no one existed beside him.

He sought to guide ignorant followers with many elegant compositions, yet they were full of errors and lacked even a slight trace of doubt-resolution; compared to the ancestral Way, it seems he had never been touched by it at all.

As for those who have arrogantly assumed names and titles, they too have a coarse degree of attainment; I myself, during the Shao-ding era, retired from San-shan and was improperly appointed to the seat of the Hu-xin monastery.
One day, he suddenly came to visit me, producing from his sleeve a single scroll of literary drafts he had composed, saying he sought my verification.
His intention was to display his skill in composition, yet I have long known that he does not recognize his own limits and recklessly produces such unworthy works.

To speak of the wondrous and discourse on the profound without any basis is like a village dweller from a distant land boasting to the capital, or an ugly woman describing her youthful beauty—utterly lacking in modesty.
I am precisely like a sober man looking upon a drunken one; I shall not trouble myself to adjudicate their right or wrong.
Having placed this upon my desk for several years, I have now composed a brief work to indicate a few points therein.
Having been unworthily entangled in worldly positions, I was returning [to my roots] when I did not yet know whether this text was still circulating.
At the beginning of the Chunyou era, while at the Fangzhang Hall of Cangzhou, I suddenly obtained the "Household Legacy of Zhongnan. Upon seeing its title, I could not contain my joy and admiration;
how could I have known that such a treasure existed within our school? When I finally unrolled the scroll and began to read it, I found that the opening chapter was exactly as I had expected.
In the opening section of the *Huaijia zizhuan*, it is stated that our patriarch propagated the Vinaya with "sublime contemplation" as its foundation.

This implies that within the Vinaya itself, the application of mindfulness and contemplation for remediation—such as constantly maintaining a single-minded recollection to eliminate the various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*)—is already present;

however, because these still belong to the category of "lesser contemplation," he introduced the sublime contemplation of the *Vijñaptimātratā* (Consciousness-Only) to guide it as the foundation for propagating the Vinaya. Yet, it remains uncertain whether our patriarch’s primary intent was to propagate the Vinaya.

Is it for the sake of propagating *vipaśyanā* (contemplation)? If you say it is for propagating the *vinaya*, why does the *vinaya* lack a foundational text? If you say it is for propagating *vipaśyanā*, why speak of propagating the *vinaya*?
To say that both are propagated depends on the person; regarding their practice, there is neither "acceptable" nor "unacceptable.

Since you have already stated that propagating the *vinaya* is precisely according to the teaching (*śāsana*), and since the teaching has its own basis, why must one borrow a foundational text to sever [doubts] regarding the mind? This is intended to demonstrate that our school is not a study of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

This means that one who is capable of eliminating, thoroughly investigating, transcending, and uprooting suffering is a worthy person; how could such a person fail to know? On the contrary, it is the ignorant mind that plays with cleverness until it becomes clumsy.

Regarding the clothing, food, four modes of deportment, and various precepts discussed in the text, the points concerning the application of the mind for their remediation must be fully realized during daily activities;

thus, the rules and methods are exhaustively detailed to correctly clarify the practice of the precepts. Those who claim this is "sublime contemplation" are deluded by the name and do not understand the reality.

In what regard is the precept maintained? It is discussed as the mind-ground being true within phenomena; only by eliminating [deluded] positions can one reach this stage. Furthermore, how could one forget the precepts?

The patriarchal teachings were exclusively propagated for the sake of those who are newly learning. To eliminate ignorance and clarify contemplative wisdom, the conditions of objects are provisionally shown.

This is established according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) to complete the substance of receiving the precepts. Regarding the phenomena of good and evil, one should correctly practice them with reverence.

The holding consciousness, confronting the five sensory objects, does not tolerate even the slightest trace [of defilement]; it requires that one’s stage of broad practice (*bhūmi*) initiate the departure toward realization and know the place of return.

Although the Great and Small Vehicles differ, their ethical discipline (*vinaya*) is no different. They converge in the three aggregates (*triskandha*) and perfectly accord with the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). To receive and follow this as the Way is not the same as worldly goodness;

therefore, both the *Śū* (Commentary) and the *Cāo* (Sub-commentary) open up the Mahāyāna understanding by taking the realm of the Dharma-dhātu as the object and generating the superior grade of mind to embrace it.
The substance of the wholesome seeds gives rise to the bodhisattva practices that lead toward the fruit of nirvana;

through the exhaustive application of the perfect and real Mahāyāna teachings, one receives the śrāvaka’s minor precepts without distinguishing between the two. Thus, the provisional is taken as the real, with beginning and end forming a single thread, so that the ultimate karma may be accomplished.
Since the sequence described in the "Chapter on the Substance of the Precepts" within the Perfect School (*Yuanzong*) is not unclear, the text states: "Wisdom knows."

"Objects and conditions are originally created by the mind; do not falsely take objects as conditions, but recognize that there is only a single consciousness which transforms according to conditions, such that 'that' exists and 'this' exists.
(Text) This first demonstrates objects and conditions to open up great understanding. Furthermore, it says: "If one wishes to comprehend deluded emotions, one must know deluded karma;

therefore, performing actions and receiving [precepts] further perfumes the deluded mind. (Text) Based on this understanding, one takes objects as conditions to resolve the mind and receive the precepts. Furthermore, it says:

That which becomes the seeds of goodness within the fundamental storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is the essence of this precept (text). This correctly demonstrates the essence of the precepts generated by the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*).
The preceding section is identical to the *Chao* (Commentary). Regarding the phrase "I now resolve my mind to receive the precepts":

it means employing one’s own resolute intention to correspond with that wondrous Dharma; within that Dharma, there is the principle of causal origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which is received and held within the mind.

It is called the "precept-substance" (*śīla-tattva*). Furthermore, because before receiving the precepts, evil pervaded the entire *dharmadhātu*, and now, desiring to advance in receiving them, one overturns that previous state of evil by giving rise to a wholesome mind, the cause for the emergence of the precepts likewise pervades the *dharmadhātu*. (Text) It also says:

"Because there still exists the measure of the original seed-mind, its power is constant," and so on, down to: "it accomplishes the transformation-body Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*)," etc. (Text) This clarifies the accordance [with reality].

The two passages— "Practicing the observances and transgressions with the instruction to constantly contemplate the distant goal" and "In order to accomplish the three clusters of precepts (*tri-skandhaka-śīla*),

one proceeds toward the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣa*) to seek the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, and furthermore, uses this Dharma to guide sentient beings"— correspond to one another like the joining of tally-sticks.

Regarding the distinction between receiving [the precepts] later versus contemplating them beforehand within the context of the three clusters alone, it would not be possible [to understand them] were it not for Ji.

Although the responses to the *Yuan* (Circumstantial) [section] recognize the far-reaching intent of the Perfect School (*yuanzong*), the Mahāyāna cause and effect elucidated in these two sections are both subsumed within the three vows.
Within the substance of non-productive karma (*avijñapti-karma*) generated by the reception of the full precepts, there is already that which causes one to rely upon and practice them;

the present text now definitively clarifies this. Therefore, the *Ji yuan* (Resolving the Circumstances) states: "Now, this directly uses the perfect meaning of Mahāyāna to resolve the substance mentioned previously."

The *Karmavācanā-sūtra* cites the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* as an authoritative teaching, stating: "Whenever one wishes to receive the precepts, one must first be instructed with the Dharma to open their understanding, so that they may give rise to compassion toward all objects;
only then can they attain the karma of the superior precepts (*adhiśīla*). The *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) states:

"This dharma of the precepts is the fundamental duty of those who have left the household life; it is not something for those who harbor great [worldly] attachments, nor can it easily be contained by those who are difficult to discipline, except in cases where there is a specific cause."
The fundamental principle of the Vinaya is that its essential practice is truly contained herein; if one seeks it elsewhere, one moves further away from the Way.

Regarding the source of the Buddhist teachings for those seeking salvation, it is said that the teaching is the Vinaya-piṭaka, and since the Vinaya arises from the precepts (*śīla*), the precepts are the foundation of the Vinaya.

As for the three types of contemplation on principle according to the scriptures of the patriarchal teachings, they should be applied where appropriate. In the two gates of the precepts and contemplation, [the following] must be observed:

One distinguishes between mind and object: taking the precepts as the mind and the prohibition of evil as the object; taking contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) as the mind and the principle of quiescence (*śamatha*) as the object.

Although there are phrases regarding the arising and ceasing of phenomena within the object of contemplation, these refer to the phenomenal object—such as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*’s statement that "all dharmas arise from causes and conditions"—and do not refer to the ultimate truth (*satya*).
If one were to correlate the two levels of subject and object, then the contemplation of truth would belong [to the latter].
That which is to be refuted must be observed with clarity, like a vessel; only when one is simple and sincere can it be called "wondrous observation.
Furthermore, one must know that the method for cultivating observation specifically points to a single object, allowing no other thoughts.

As recorded in the *New Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation* by the Master [Zhiyi], the three dharmas are taken from the broad to the narrow—focusing on the mind and focusing on the Buddha—to precisely select the object of observation. Thus, the object of observation accords with the four types of success.

How could it be appropriate to permit negligence? Although the *Sixteen Contemplations* (Shiliu guanmen) is originally from a single scripture, its textual expression does not yet reach the contemplations themselves;

rather, at the conclusion of each contemplation, the section is formally concluded. Regarding the general outline of Tiantai, the four samādhis categorize and encompass the teachings of a lifetime of scriptures.

What is elucidated therein clarifies that the three great works (*Sandaibu*) primarily belong to the category of "contemplation through practice" (*xingguan*), while the other two works are all categorized as "opening" (*kai*).

Although the "Exegesis" (*Jie*) employs contemplation by relying on events and attaching to phenomena, the first six chapters within the "Contemplation of the Mind" still pertain to wondrous understanding (*miaojie*).
In the section that correctly clarifies the object, it takes a single thought-moment among the events as the object of contemplation, using the Three Thousand Worlds exclusively as a guide.
Based on the sutras, it establishes the expedient practice of formal cultivation, sets a time limit for establishing meditative concentration, and breaks through delusion to reveal the truth.
In contemplating the realms and penetrating the realms through investigation, one must clarify the ten realms (*daśa-viṣaya*) in order to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox;

the gravity with which the practice of contemplation is generally approached is roughly like this. Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka is divided into schools: the Sūtra-piṭaka elucidates the study of concentration (*samādhi*), specifically clarifying meditative absorption;

the Vinaya-piṭaka elucidates the study of precepts (*śīla*), dealing exclusively with upholding and violating them; and the Abhidharma-piṭaka elucidates the study of wisdom (*prajñā*), which opens up the two types of knowledge (*jñāna*)—it is not that these are absent.

When these are combined, they are all termed the "Precepts of Following Speech" (*anuvāda-śīla*). When the training in precepts (*śīla-śikṣā*) reaches its ultimate consummation, it is the "Three Collections" (*tri-saṃvara*);

when the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*) reaches its ultimate consummation, it is "Consciousness-Only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) (this being according to our own school). All of these are capable of reaching the fruit and equally accomplish the Buddha-wisdom. Precepts without wisdom and understanding are merely sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*);

contemplation without wisdom and understanding belongs to mundane dhyāna (*dharma-citta*). Precepts are that which can prevent karma and are that which is prevented; contemplation is that which can cultivate.

Since that which is cultivated definitely belongs to the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), whether it be precepts, karma, contemplation, or dhyāna, there is not a single dharma that does not reach the stage of fruition.

Thus, within the texts of this school, some clarify liberating wisdom and demonstrate the accomplishment of principle-contemplation for the sake of receiving and following the wondrous precepts of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*).

For these reasons, the commentaries (*shu* and *chao*) sometimes refer to the shallow and deep levels of the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*), and sometimes refer to the sharpness or dullness of one's faculties (*indriya*).

Comparing the three vehicles and the three trainings against one another, resolving their distinctions, and conceptualizing them as belonging to the opening of understanding constitute the fundamental duty of the renunciant, with the goal of accomplishing the Noble Path.

The term "renunciation" must be understood in terms of the person and the practice; when discussing its initial cultivation, it does not refer merely to the precepts or to specific stages, for it is practiced from the very beginning and cuts off [defilements] immediately.
Therefore, the sections on Receiving Precepts and the Śrāmaṇera Chapter state that the Noble Path practice begins from this very origin.
Never before has it been so clear that this is the first step for entering the Way; one must know the direction toward which to proceed and ensure that one advances in study.

Within the section on repentance (*chān*), three types of contemplation based on principle (*lǐguān*) are listed, allowing one to observe according to one's wisdom. One should practice both the transformative (*huà*) and the restrictive (*zhì*) disciplines together to eliminate the root of karma.

Furthermore, regarding what is extinguished—even down to the commission of offenses—one must guide them through integration to achieve "repentance of non-arising" (*wúshēng chàn*), which differs from the prohibitive nature of mere ritual precepts (*jìxíng*).

Arising thoughts are not constant; one must prevent and restrain them, for they cannot be permitted through deluded emotions. One should understand that the two aspects of precept and contemplation are to be practiced in this way.

Our Patriarch established the teachings to open up the wisdom and understanding of the Mahāyāna, yet he specifically relied upon the Hīnayāna for receiving and following the precepts, in which there is nothing that is not perfectly excellent. In all four modes of conduct and every movement, one must maintain strict protection and observance.

Clearly understand that based on the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), even if one indulges in delusion, karma is formed; if one wishes to turn back from delusion, [one must apply these methods].

Since the violations of the precepts were eliminated through the methods established by Yuan, his strict prohibitions became even more earnest. These precepts are the supreme practice; why then speak of them as "sublime contemplation"?
Thus, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts) states: "They form the seeds of goodness"—this refers to the essence of the precepts (*śīla*).

For ordinary beings who, through deluded thoughts, cling to false objects, there is no way to attain liberation except through the understanding of the precepts. Therefore, the *Lüxu* (Preface to the Vinaya) says: "Bondage arises from this; through this, liberation is perfected."
The subtle principle of contemplating the Buddha-ground has never been false; now, for those at the stage of initial resolve, it is made the fundamental basis. How can one practice and advance?

One must understand that by comprehending delusion, one realizes the absolute truth—this is something one cannot fail to know. "From the very beginning, there was never [delusion]"—truly, these words are sincere.

If Master Tie had ever applied his mind to the contemplation of the precepts, even if he had merely gathered some fragments of it, he would never have fallen into this state. Yuanji’s deluded talk shows that he does not recognize his own limits.

The boastful, arrogant, and delusory remarks found in the subsequent sections, as well as the provisional instructions for "gathering the source" (*huìyuán*) and the characters annotated beneath the headings of the various gateways (*mén*), must be urgently removed;
I fear they will mislead beginners and lead them to groundless self-restraint. It is of great benefit for those at the initial stage of practice to recite and study the original text.
As for the established topical outlines (*biāokē*) and the various sub-commentaries, they mostly follow the author’s own views and cannot be relied upon entirely.
I am now old and weary, lacking the heart to read with meticulous care; were I to live for several more years, it might serve as a tether.

As I examine the merits of contemplative practice (*guanxing*), I see that the ancestral Way of the Vinaya school has been buried. Regarding the fundamental nature of the true and the false, my ancestors’ own writings provide their own standards.

Nevertheless, works such as the *Guijing yi* (Ritual of Paying Homage) and the *Jingxin guan* (Contemplation of Purifying the Mind) encompass both wisdom and practice, perfecting the school’s doctrine. Thus, the teachings of transformation (*hua*) and regulation (*zhi*) are propagated together in truth.

Although worldly conventions allow for the general inclusion of both ordinary study and the contemplation of capacities, this belongs to the gate of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), where there is no confusion with the regulations of the Vinaya (*vinaya-śāsana*).
The intent of the Patriarchs regarding the transmission of the schools can be understood; thus, [your] hasty arrival does not accord with the correct measure.

To single out its errors and excesses would be beyond words: first, the study of the Vinaya lacks its foundation; second, the gates of transformation and regulation are not distinguished; third, the sequence of the three studies is lost; fourth...

This causes later generations who study the path to: (1) fail to fully grasp the five means of gathering sentient beings; (2) not recognize the fundamental tenet; (3) bring disgrace upon the ancestral masters; (4) remain utterly confused regarding the characteristics of the precepts;
(5) obscurely rely on the gate of contemplation; and (6) falsely claim to differ from other paths. Briefly cited here are these ten points, yet their failures are still many more.

Because of this, my heart was offended and I could no longer bear to look at it further. At the end of the year, I went to the ordination platform and suddenly heard the teachings of the Ancestral Master being upheld.

The discourse on discarding the *Śīla-saṃvara* and accepting the "Great" [teachings] already deviates from what has been studied and is utterly alien to the ear. Upon returning to the temple after descending from the altar, I happened to encounter the phrase "restoring the circle" (*chóngyuán*).
Seeing this master of disorder overturning the fourfold pavilion and claiming that its meaning was "completely opened," I could not help but feel profound sorrow and lamentation.
To destroy the Mahāyāna and slander the ancestral teachings is to have no fear at all for the bitter retributions of the hells.

If you say that because the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* reveals the "white fourfold" [precepts] as requiring the gradual attainment of the great wholesome precepts, it is therefore a perversion to claim otherwise—

then you do not understand that once the five meanings of the Perfect Gate are revealed, why would [the practitioner] not alone reach the four-story pavilion? You do not realize that this very revelation is precisely for the sake of this.
I venture to ask: regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*, does its revelation and manifestation open only for the śrāvakas or also for the bodhisattvas?
Among the many types of śrāvakas, which ones attain Buddhahood through this revelation? How does it reveal and manifest according to the specific capacity of the audience?

What is the essential purport of this revelation and manifestation? How do our Patriarchs and the present school establish this doctrine? Furthermore, after the revelation and manifestation, are there still śrāvaka teachings to be practiced?
Regarding the aforementioned matters, those who have not studied them remain in total ignorance; they deceive the common folk with empty clamor, skillfully manipulating their lips and tongues.

With a single blast of factional wind, they cast doubt upon the entire assembly. When the *Sūtra of Good Precepts* is being recited, no one dares to speak of it; thus the Dharma is extinguished and the Patriarchs are slandered, leaving the ignorant masses blind and deluded.
How can such things be endured? What indeed cannot be endured? He then exerted his strength to break through this darkness to rescue the ancestral vehicle, relying on the conditions of that new era.

I have long admired [him], yet when he came to seek instruction for his students, I merely composed a single letter to provide admonition. He prepared the formalities and engaged in a dialogue, but since his conduct was superficial, I did not take it to heart.
Subsequently, whenever we met, there was almost no sign of him appreciating my words.

I considered that one who hears the righteous should be able to change their ways; thus, I remained indifferent even as he grew old among our clan. Later, I heard that he had produced a work titled "Breaking the Thatch" (*Zhěpéng*), but I had no means to see it. Recently, because of... [text fragment].

To see one who leads the blind and whose cultivation is merely perfunctory, and who lacks any personal insight yet allows himself to be dragged along by others, to then widely print and circulate [his work]—this is truly extraordinary.
Having obtained a copy of this "One Family" (Ekavyavahārika) school, I read it once and it caused me great doubt;

I read it a second time and it was enough to make me laugh; I read it a third time and it filled me with extreme concern. Based on his refutations and explanations, how could they suffice as a refutation? To the clear-eyed, they are nothing more than a mockery.
I have been a source of ridicule before others; however, I fear that in this degenerate age, those among the new students who understand will be few.

Because they are thus deluded, they will fail to investigate the source and its currents to the utmost, and over time, various factions will form. If I do not point out these errors, the ancestral vehicle (*zǔchéng*) will gradually be obscured;

if it is not transmitted to future generations, it will surely become a grave harm. Unable to refrain from further speech, I shall briefly set forth what I know to show to those who come after; this is not for my own sake.
Excellent.

To clarify this intent, one must first establish the fundamental basis: it should be known that the present practice of receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*) is based on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, yet it is capable of eliminating [the limitations of mere ritual] by employing the perfect and ultimate teachings of the *Yuan-shi* (Perfect Reality) school;
it reaches back to the original intention of the Tathāgata, taking the objective realm as its condition and accords with the vehicle of the *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) school.

Generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one gives rise to the supreme practice of great compassion; clarifying the mind and its objects, one guides them toward integration. This essential vow of the gate of awakening leaves nothing behind, as it aims for the vast and far-reaching.

The meaning of the "unconditioned" (anabhisaṃskāra) that has been generated possesses the three clusters (*triskandha*), and because the substance of the karma accomplished thereby is identical to the substance of the Mahāyāna, the *Commentary* states:
"I cause [them] to generate the aspiration and receive the precepts so that the three clusters of precepts may be perfected; thus they proceed toward the three gates of liberation. Correct.
The *Petition for the Fruit of Nirvāṇa* states: "Therefore, the practitioner should constantly contemplate this practice; it is precisely the 'Three Collections' (tri-skandha).
Since the mind of understanding is already subtle, there should be no limitation in its manifestation. As vows and practice support one another, the mind finds its domain.
When discussing its name and rank, such a person is a Śrāvaka who possesses the disposition of a Great Śrāvaka; they can only be called a Bodhisattva who has newly resolved their mind."

As the *Puming pusa jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Samantaprabha) states: "Just as when a Kṣatriya king, even if he has illicit relations with a low-born woman, the child conceived is noble and is called a prince;

so too, when one who has produced the supreme aspiration for the Dharma, even if they have united with a lowly person among sentient beings, gives birth to the bodhicitta, they are called a son of the Buddha.
(Scriptural Text) The term "sentient beings" refers to those in the nine realms, namely: humans, devas, and those of the minor wholesome categories, as well as the views and adornments.

The king, the evil and rebellious Devadatta, and others have all been revealed to become Buddhas; now this supreme arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment is joined with the "thief-like" śrāvakas and the "lady.
The seeds of karma thus aroused possess the potential to achieve Buddhahood, because the perfect principle contains and encompasses all without exception.
Thus, even these minor precepts are perfected in their own place, such that from the initial stage up to the fruit of Buddhahood, the essence of the name does not change. If one takes this...
The essence [of the precepts] constitutes the essence of a bodhisattva; conversely, when one views the śrāvaka [precepts], this perfect essence is absent.

Therefore, the Master feared confusion regarding this and posed questions at every stage throughout the various texts. Whether this [śrāvaka] essence is identical to or different from the essence of the bodhisattva precepts, there must be some difference;

let students investigate this. Some say that while the essence is the same, the conditions (ālambana) are different; yet to speak only of their identity already implies they are two distinct essences.

How much more so when it is said that the conditions are different? An ancient master stated: "What is called 'identity of substance' (*tītóng*) is based on the essential nature (*tǐxìng*); if one speaks in terms of the phenomenal characteristics (*tǐxiàng*), they are likewise not the same.

In the Perfect Principle (*yuánlǐ*), all phenomena are fully present; the phenomena are entirely identical, yet there is no confusion among them. If they were mixed into a single unity, how could there be "fully present phenomena"? As the Sūtra says:
"The great chariots of the seven treasures are immeasurable in number. Someone asked: "Since one has already attained this essence (*tǐ*), does one still use it to receive Bodhi?"
Question: Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, must one receive them again, or is it sufficient to rely on a general judgment of their observance or violation?
Answer: One must receive them. Question: Is there no need for a renewed formal act (*anabhisamskāra*)? Answer:

If it were as you say—that once this essence has been attained, there is no need to receive them again—then why do you not rely on the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and other texts to uphold them according to their specific modes of practice, but instead willingly commit violations of the various precepts? You say that you have...

"Does Śākyamuni still look at the sutras? If one relies on your false interpretation, where would there be 'nothing acceptable' or 'nothing unacceptable,' and where would there be 'no weighty action'?

It is precisely because of your delusion that a fleeting thought arises, causing you to fall into the Avīci Hell. Since you possess the full conditions for receiving great retribution, how could there not be 'unmanifest action' (avijñapti)?

As it is fundamentally perfect and ultimate, its meaning is already complete; there is only one set of three groups of pure precepts (tri-śikṣā-saṃvara), not two sets of three. This is because you have received the Great [Vehicle]."
To preface its meaning here: it is like throwing water into the ocean or blowing air into a bellows; even one with the wisdom of a Great Sage could not distinguish them.

Yet, when they are gathered together in great measure, there is no distinction among the three aggregates (*tri-skandha*). Were it not for the Master of Prophecy (*Vyākaraṇa-ācārya*), who possesses the eye of the discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*) and has profoundly mastered both the transformative and the restrictive teachings, who could clarify this?
To break through the foolish attachments of those as ignorant as reeds, one must know that within the Sūtras there are fields.
A man abandoned his son and saw a nobleman putting salt into his food. He asked, "Why do you do this? The nobleman replied, "This salt makes it delicious.
The man thought to himself, "It is indeed delicious," and since he had not yet eaten much, he proceeded to fill his mouth with it.
Suffering from the extreme saltiness, he turned back to reproach the nobleman. The nobleman said, "Foolish man! Salt is for seasoning; how can you eat it alone?"
They, too, are likewise of a single flavor; yet, being attached to the excellence of perfect bliss, they do not know the reason for that perfection and excellence.
If my ancestors’ noble wisdom were to rely on and follow the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) according to its own specific division, they would still be halfway there and not have reached the ultimate goal.

Alternatively, if one causes them to take the first step directly toward the Great Square (Mahāyāna), then when receiving the Bodhisattva precepts according to the Mahāyāna sūtras, their practice will be long-lasting and their capacity far-reaching.

If one has not yet fulfilled the Great Practice and the Difficult Practices, one will ultimately fall back; therefore, having deeply discerned the suitability of the capacity, one receives the Śrāvaka precepts with a Mahāyāna mind.
This is not for the sake of counting jewels, but truly to bring success to the task. There is a great reason for this progressive advancement so that one does not abandon the path midway;

He asked again: "Are the three clusters (triskandha) and the three bodies (trikāya) identical or distinct? Are the words different while the meaning is one? The three bodies are precisely the three clusters and the three vows;
the Buddha-mind and the Buddha-body are without difference, and cause and effect are non-dual. Only one who can realize this may be called a possessor of the perfect precepts (pariśuddha-śīla).
These are the *pāramitās* and the ultimate liberation (*mokṣa*). Thus, it should be known that if a practitioner gives rise to this mind and attains this essence," [the goal is achieved].

This is precisely the seed of the Buddhas of the three periods, as recorded in the preceding text; whether cause or fruit, whether for one’s own practice or for transforming others, all are the substance of the vow.
Possessing these various dharmas is like the earth possessing peach and plum trees: though they have not yet sprouted from the soil, how could their branches and leaves not be luxuriant?
As for "the seeds of the goodness of cultivation and nature," this is that very meaning. This directly reveals the perfect endowment of the mind and karma.
How can these characteristics be considered already established as the three clusters (*tri-rāśi*)?

If they were indeed the ultimate three clusters, they would also have to be the ultimate three Buddhas, with all immeasurable Dharma-gates manifesting before one; this would mean that Maitreya is spontaneously natural and Śākyamuni is spontaneously natural.
Why, then, does the Patriarch [Hongren] say below that "cultivating and manifesting is called the Dharmakāya Buddha"? How could it be that by means of the precepts one has aroused...?

Since the substance [of this vow] is already established as cause and effect, the commentators have indulged in arbitrary speculations regarding its nature. This substance is explained in terms of its full possession;

that is, it is entrusted to one to constantly contemplate and remember. The Master [Daoxuan] said: "This practice is the śrāvaka precept produced by the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion and three proclamations).

Because one undertakes and receives it by making a vow in accordance with the perfect principle, the substance of this vow is able to encompass all dharmas. This was stated previously in the section on the conditions for receiving the precepts. Regarding this—
The precepts and the monastic life are fundamentally not intended for those who harbor great resolve; that they cannot easily accommodate such depth has its reasons.
Furthermore, if one does not rely on compassion, how can one contain a great intention? This point will be addressed later. Later, he concludes by pointing out:

"Now, recognizing the prior conditions, one returns to the city of the Mahāyāna; because the mind dwells therein, we know that the entirety of the Patriarch’s writings from beginning to end is centered upon this."

Regarding the establishment of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) based on the formal reception [of the precepts], this practice is intended precisely for those who have already received the Great [Precepts].

However, those who wish to fulfill the three clusters of sublime precepts (*tripuṇya-śīla*) yet are entirely unable to grasp the great purport of the Buddha-dharma, do nothing more than desire to receive the Great [Precepts] through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the four-part formal motion). They claim that once the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is concluded, their thoughts and vows are satisfied and their expectations fully realized, thereby fulfilling the three clusters. This is a grave error.

It is merely an attempt to establish the Great [Precepts] through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, while simultaneously discarding the four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*) of the wholesome precepts. As they say: "When the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is finished, one's contemplation and aspiration are fulfilled, and what was expected is smoothly accomplished; thus the three clusters are attained."
Is it not ultimately the case that this is the place where the supreme grade of great accomplishment is received?

Question: At the time of the formal *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion and three-fold proclamation), is one to employ compassion directed toward a specific object (*ālambana-maitrī*)? Answer: It is not employed.

Since the essence of the unconditioned action (*anabhisaṃskāra-karma*) does not arise from a specific object, if one were to employ such directed compassion, why would the Patriarch’s commentary state, "As for the direction [of the mind]..."? If this were the case, it would be precisely for the purpose of receiving [the precepts] at this time.
What did the Great Patriarch mean when he said, "The meaning lies in what follows"? The present discussion concerns the vows established upon receiving the precepts;

it is not merely the precepts issued against newly arisen evils, nor is it solely the conduct practiced through the *vinaya* discipline, nor is it exclusively for the sake of the fruit accomplished for oneself.

It does not abide in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*). To perfect this complete capacity, one is fit to receive [the precepts]. As the *Dachao* says: "It is for the purpose of accomplishing the three clusters (*triskandha*). This is its intended meaning.

If one asks, "Is it not necessary to receive [the precepts] in order for them to be effective? This is indeed so, for in the past our former masters took the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) in its entirety as the Mahāyāna.
Thus, the *Zizhi* (Fundamental Commentary) refutes this by asking: "If the Four-Part Vinaya is the Mahāyāna, why is it considered 'Small'?

It further argues that the essence and practice of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* are entirely identical to those of the Bodhisattva and Śrāvaka precepts, and there is no distinction between them; yet one must know that this is certainly not the case. Therefore, the intended meaning of the Patriarch’s words follows from...
The meaning of "accommodating" (*yōng*) should be understood as partially accommodating the profound [Mahāyāna] while supporting and developing the intent [of the Hīnayāna].

Furthermore, it was asked: "Regarding those of superior capacity (*śreṣṭha-adhimukti*), are they entirely Mahāyāna, or only partially accommodating? The answer was: "It supports and establishes the meaning of partial accommodation within our own school.

Now, that [text] instead claims: "Those of superior capacity receive the Great [Vehicle]; although this is originally a case of partial accommodation, in the end it is established as being restricted to the development [of the Mahāyāna]."
If the "perfectly decisive" (yuanjue) [vow] is established as being of the superior grade within the "partially universal" (fentong), why is it said that one receives the Small [Vehicle]?

Why is it said that the superior-grade arousal of the mind constitutes the meaning of the Perfect [Vehicle]? And why is it said that although it is originally partially universal, the "perfectly decisive" is further established?

One must know that the superior-grade perfect reception is precisely intended to reveal that the "partially universal" of our own school is, in fact, no different from the three [vehicles]. Thus, the superior grade of the Perfect School is identical to the partially universal; there is no distinction between them.

The three clusters (*tri-skandha*) of the Mahāyāna are fundamentally and originally perfect; why, then, would they need to be established separately? It is only because this "Great" [vehicle] exists within the "Small" that they are distinguished as partial applications (*pradeśa-prasara*).

If one were to definitively attain the Great, there would likewise be no need for a separate establishment. Thus, Jieyuan says: "Since they are already partial applications, why must they be established separately? The answer is:
although the meaning is indeed pervasive of the Great, the manifestation ultimately remains confined to the Small. To avoid confusing them with the universal, they must be established.

Regarding the separate establishment [of this category], a detailed examination of that teaching reveals three points of impossibility: first, that the superior grade of perfect reception (*paripūrṇa-samādāna*) constitutes the Small Vehicle rather than the Great;

second, that the superior grade is itself the Perfect [Vehicle] and cannot be divided into two; and third, that since the definitive meaning is universally applicable, how can it be said to be restricted?

As the *Fajiji* states, "The development [of the aspiration] is restricted to the Small," is this not clearly evident? Therefore, one should know that while the superior grade of perfect reception is inclusive of the Great when expanded, it is the Small when contracted.
Regarding the brief summary, the *Four-Part Vinaya Commentary* states: "I now receive the precepts in order to fulfill the three clusters of precepts (*tri-saṃvara*).
What is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of these three clusters of precepts? The *Ratnakūṭa-alaṃkāra-sūtra* says: 'The Bodhisattva’s practice is fully encompassed by the three clusters.

Regarding the cluster of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), it is the restraint that prohibits evil; because it ultimately severs the karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) of bondage. Regarding the cluster of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*),"
Because it is the ultimate cultivation and realization of both mundane and supramundane, great and small practices, it gathers in sentient beings by ultimately delivering all conscious beings.
If one merely arouses the mind through vows without relying on the sutras to receive the subtle [teachings], this is but a vain production of understanding;

such vows will not constitute the Great Precepts. Regarding the observance and violation of these precepts, the Sutra commands that one seek a teacher for a thousand *li*; how could one permit such changes? This is now...
Ordinary beings have not yet realized the fruits [of the path], and their ethical conduct is likewise deficient; although they must single-mindedly strive for progress, as the ancients said:
"Understanding may be fully manifested, but practice requires gradual cultivation."

Question: Since it is necessary to practice gradually, I fear this may obstruct the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching]. Answer: One practices gradually all day long, yet one advances perfectly all day long.

If it were otherwise, even a person of the Perfect Teaching at the First Abode would still have forty grades of ignorance remaining unbroken; they would still need to sever them gradually—would this not be the Perfect Teaching?

It is when the Buddhas and Patriarchs correctly manifest this that it becomes straightforward and clear; when those of heterodox views speak of it, it becomes a heterodox teaching, as mentioned above.
Although the intention of the Venerable Zu Wenzheng was clear, his application of a "heart of wild weeds" (*péngxīn*) and his tortuous, artificial interpretations may mislead future generations.

Without discussing the slant or correctness [of his views], he further cites commentaries and sub-commentaries to add another layer of explanation. In the *Karmavācanā-sūtra*, it first quotes the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*:
"Whenever one wishes to receive the precepts, one must give rise to a mind of compassion toward all objects; thus, one attains the *adhiśīla* (higher morality)."
Question: The many treatises cited belong to the Sarvāstivāda school; thus, the arising of compassion and the receiving of the precepts constitute a "partial" (fen-tong) meaning. Answer:
It is said that while various schools occasionally held this view, it was not as explicit as the five meanings found in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Now, to assist in clarifying this perspective, the intent of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is not merely the initial arousal of the thought [of enlightenment]. Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, did not disdain the shallow pond.

Question: Now that it is established that one must possess the three vows as precepts to give rise to the superior grade of the Perfect [Vehicle], why does the text on the Three Precepts merely state "arising compassion" and "ceasing [harm]" as the means for saving sentient beings?

Answer: The *Ji yuan* states: "Although the three precepts each fully possess the five [precepts], when it comes to their practice and observance, they are constantly used to encompass and save living beings;
thus they can freely employ and include all things—how could they stop at merely gathering the remaining aggregates? The Treatise says: "In general..."
Regarding the desire to receive the precepts, since it is said that "all who desire [them]," there is no selection between great or small capacities;

this applies not only to the *Dharmaguptaka* school but serves as the primary practice for those on the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and is the fundamental duty of one who has left the household life (*pravrajita*). The commentators have grasped the essential meaning in their sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) and explain the text as follows:

"This dharma of the precepts is the fundamental duty of one who has left the household life; it was never originally intended for those who harbor the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna), and it is certainly difficult for them to contain within themselves. There is a profound reason for this. This explains the preceding point.
This precept-dharma relies on the treatises to give rise to compassion; thus, one mounts the initial practice and remains undeluded regarding the Dharma. Furthermore, it is said:

"If one previously did not take compassion as an object, how could one now accommodate the Great Meaning? This refers to what follows. To explain the above: the fundamental duty of the renunciant is to aspire toward the far-reaching and vast.

To achieve this, nothing is better than bending the *pōng* grass [to make a roof]; one must employ skillful means to develop this aspiration. Having no choice but to explain this dharma, I shall now turn back.
I reproach myself for my shallow attainment; how could it compare to that of my elder brother?

As stated in the *Śīla-sūtra* and the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra*, these are precisely what is received by the seven classes of followers. Previously, I did not rely on compassion; how could I have harbored such a grand intention?
This point will be explained further below.

The passage from the *Péngyún shū* (Péngyún’s Commentary) stating "the family [of the practitioner] is precisely the scriptural evidence" refers to the words of the cited authority; why would you need to state this? The Patriarch did not cite this as evidence;
your claim is a false assertion. The Master of the Record himself stated: "According to the intent of this sutra, anyone who becomes a bhikṣu must necessarily receive the Bodhisattva Great Precepts.
Thus, receiving the Small Precepts first is for the purpose of generating the compassionate conditions for receiving the Great Precepts later; the intention lies in what follows.

Furthermore, you, sir, as soon as you see a citation, immediately claim that others establish the dharma based on the sūtras and receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), falsely asserting that they "arouse compassion to receive the great" while having a basis for what they have inherited.

Yet, [the text] says "arouse compassion to receive the small"—what then is meant by "receiving the great"? It is precisely because the record states "arouse compassion to receive the small" that it allows for the subsequent reception of the great;
therefore, the commentary and records provide a false and biased interpretation to show that [the sūtra] was never [actually cited]. If it were a sūtra...
There is not a single word in the original text that can be interpreted according to your arbitrary and false exegesis.

If the sevenfold precepts were themselves the Bodhisattva precepts, what would be the purpose of establishing a "root"? It would simply have been said: "The seven groups of followers receive [the precepts];
those who receive the sevenfold group precepts but do not receive the Bodhisattva precepts possess only the capacity for receiving [the precepts], but lack the dharma that is received."

Péngyún: Since it is permitted for the seven assemblies to receive the Bodhisattva precepts, why should there be doubt regarding a bhikṣu receiving the full precepts and embracing the Great [Vehicle]?

Aside from you alone, who has ever not permitted the seven assemblies to receive the Bodhisattva precepts? As for a bhikṣu receiving the full precepts and embracing the Great [Vehicle], what is the point of this formal announcement (jñapti)?
It is like a plague-stricken person whose demonic possession has not yet receded; thus they speak much nonsense and slander the Patriarchs. Ultimately, who is this person?

This is because they do not realize that "Great" (Mahāyāna) refers to the gate of arousal [of the mind], while "Perfect" (Pūrṇa) refers to the wisdom of principle. Once the wisdom is perfected, the essence of what is aroused is identical to the essence of the Mahāyāna.
In the *Commentary* (*Shu*), it is frequently stated: "The essence of this," where the word "this" is restricted by which specific scripture? The *Sub-commentary* (*Chao*) states:
"I now arouse the mind and receive the precepts in order to fulfill the Threefold Aggregate of Precepts; I proceed toward the three gates of liberation and truly seek Nirvāṇa."
Furthermore, by means of this Dharma, he guides sentient beings so that they now reach nirvana and cause the Dharma to abide for a long time;

he resolves his mind and receives the precepts, immediately giving rise to the Great Mind to accomplish the three clusters [of pure conduct] and proceed toward the three gates of liberation, truly seeking the fruit of Nirvana.
Moreover, by means of this Dharma, he guides sentient beings to lead them to nirvana and cause the Dharma to abide for a long time; he resolves his mind and receives the precepts.

To give rise to the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) for the sake of accomplishing the three aggregates (*triskandha*) and entering the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*) is to practice the Great Practice; to seek the fruit of *nirvāṇa* is to realize the Great Fruit. Furthermore, to guide sentient beings by means of this Dharma is to initiate the Great Aspiration so that they may reach *nirvāṇa*, and to cause them to return to the Great Abode.

(This corresponds to the five summaries of Tiantai. These constitute the distant aspiration regarding cause and effect among the Three Vows. (It is not known whether the foolish person understands that the Three Vows are the giving rise of the mind. Note:

The term "Three Vows" (*trisamaya*) refers to the vows of the Bodhisattva path as described in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. The "Five Summaries" (*pañcasaṃkṣepa*) of Tiantai refer to the five aspects of the Bodhisattva path: 1. The Great Vehicle, 2. The Great Practice, 3. The Great Fruit, 4. The Great Gathering of Beings, and 5. The Great Return to the Source. The correspondence here aligns these with the stages of generating the mind, practicing, attaining the fruit, gathering beings, and returning to the ultimate state. The final note critiques those who fail to recognize that the Three Vows are fundamentally the manifestation of the initial resolve (*cittotpāda*).

[Commentary: I have previously examined the *Jie-wen* (Explanations of the Sections) within the *Zi-chi* (Subsidiary Support), which divides the "threefold practice of self-cultivation" (*zizuo sanxing*) as follows:

"One who resolves their mind to receive [the precepts]" refers to the present formal reception of the Bhikṣu precepts. To accomplish the three clusters of pure conduct (*tripuṇya-skandha*) and proceed toward the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣa-mukha*), with the distant aim of the Mahāyāna Threefold Training (*triśikṣā*), constitutes the causal practice (*hetu-pratipatti*).
Seeking Great Nirvāṇa (*mahānirvāṇa*) constitutes the perfect fruition (*pariniṣpanna-phala*). (All of the above pertain to one's own practice.)

Furthermore, regarding the [practice of transforming others] below, and the [practice of discussing the Dharma] below: you say that apart from these three phrases of cited evidence, there is not a single word concerning the perception of "good precepts" (*śīla-saṃjñā*).
You have clearly never looked at the commentary, which previously explained that one must gradually proceed through the restricted stages, stating:
"As the *Śīla-sūtra* says, those who wish to receive the Bodhisattva precepts should first purify their minds and receive the precepts of the seven classes of disciples."

Those who aspire to the Bodhisattva path and wish to know the Great Precepts (Mahāśīla) must receive them gradually; this has never been stated [otherwise] in the *Bai-si* (the *Jñapticaturtha-karman*). Furthermore, the *Ji-yuan* states:
"As with the previously mentioned Good Precepts (*Kuśala-śīla*), one receives five and practices ten, etc."; yet there is not a single word regarding anything else. Is this not a deception?

Where is the scriptural passage that would supersede the Great Vehicle within the Perfect Teaching (*Yuan-zong*)? This slander is such that even cutting off one's tongue would be insufficient as a vow for it.
Regarding the statement that "it does not depend on the Great [Vehicle] for its reception," you have failed to understand the detailed exposition provided in the subsequent text.

I venture to ask: if the aforementioned conditions for receiving [the teaching] still involve the provisional and the Small [Vehicle], and if one says that the Dharma established based upon those conditions is precisely the provisional and Small [Vehicle] serving as the foundation for what is now being taught, why do you say it "still involves" them?
This is especially so if we consider the conditions that are able to give rise [to the realization].
If you have grasped this in your heart, it naturally belongs to the Perfect and Great (Yuan-da).

What do you mean by saying that the provisional and small (quan-xiao) teachings and their commentaries establish conditions in both places, citing the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* to establish "compassion arising from dependent origination" as the primary trigger for the profound holy practices?

The Master of the Record (Ji-zhu) has clearly explained that these are all strictly according to the Perfect meaning of the Mahāyāna. What further perfection could exist outside of this? You have not even looked at it, yet you still speak thus.
In my *Shangpin* (Superior Grade) discourse, although I spoke only of the density or thinness within the mind, I did not clarify its specific characteristics.

The Patriarch [Zhiyi], in accordance with the perfect reality (*yuan-shi-li*), established provisional meanings to serve as the foundation for the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-zong*). How can you say that I departed from the treatises?

Your claim that the Perfect Teaching is known solely through the passage on "establishing the essence" (*chu-ti*) shows you do not understand how the beginning and end form a single, continuous thread. This text appears in the *Yeshu* (Commentary on Practice), yet its meaning encompasses the entirety of the doctrine.

The *Wenzi Zhi* (Textual Support) analyzes the categories of substance (*ti*) and manifestation (*fa*) across the entire body of the Buddha’s teachings as the means of expression (*nengquan*). Thus, it states: "For now, we rely on the three schools of karma.
When our own school situates its position, it indicates that the relevant passage appears in the *Yeshu* (Karma Commentary).

If this is the case, then even the two schools of Emptiness (*kong*) and Existence (*you*) emerge solely from these [three]. Therefore, the *Ji* (Jingying Huiyuan) cites both the *Shu* and the *Chao* to clarify the three clusters (*sanju*) of receiving and following precepts.

At the conclusion of the section on the three bodies, it states: "Only then do we see that the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong) has a profound origin; how could it be that the Perfect Teaching arises solely from the *Yeshu*? It further says:

"The preceding [section] establishes the Dharma based on the school (zong), while the subsequent [section] establishes the Perfect [Teaching] to resolve and penetrate [the relationship between] the school and the Dharma.

This is precisely for the purpose of relying on what has been received. How could one begin to discuss resolution and penetration only after having received [the teachings], and yet divide them into 'before' and 'after'? What kind of statement is this?"
If you do not understand that the former [teaching] was provisional while the latter was received as the Perfect Teaching—

what I call my Patriarch’s attainment of the "intention" (yi) through the "function" (yong) of the Perfect [Teaching] to receive the Small [Vehicle], which is the original duty of those who leave home in the Three Vehicles and whose aspiration aims for the distant and the Great—

then since you do not yet comprehend even my words, how could you possibly grasp this Patriarch’s intent? You are a heavy obstacle to the Way, a source of confusion, and one who covers their ears while maligning the profound gates.

Come here to be alerted; you must see that there is no shame [in failing]. You should know that the *Great Meaning Commentary on the Three Collections* (*Sanju Dayi Chao*) explains from the point of generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*), while the *Sub-commentary* (*Shu*) clarifies this within the section on following the practice (*anuvṛtti*).

Ultimately, the two sections—the precepts (*śīla*) and the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*)—are mutually pervasive. One must understand the general intent rather than merely following the literal text.
Furthermore, he cites the Patriarch’s words: "The principles of the Great and Small Vehicles are not divided; from the Deer Park to the Twin Trees, they are one."
Regarding the mutual benefit of the small [vehicle], I am uncertain as to the intention behind it: does the small initiate the great, or does the great manifest the small?

Could there be an initiation apart from the regulations of the great and the small? It is because one does not recognize that this is a "great capacity" (mahāyāna-śakti) that one causes them to enter the small via the small;
whereas those of small capacity should enter via the great. This is how the three mysteries of the resultant Buddha respond to capacities, and upon which the Tiantai school relies.

Regarding the establishment of the two types of indefinite and secret arousal—how the Buddha alone can explain them—and how one awakens to the Way through these teachings and realizes it now by means of the conditions for the arousal of the precepts:
this text may refute your false attachment that one must necessarily practice contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) before being able to destroy delusions and manifest the principle.
What I call the "Chapter on Perfect Arousal" definitively clarifies that for those who have previously received [the precepts], since the former was established in relation to...

Because the Perfect Teaching (En) is discussed last regarding the essence [of the seeds], it can be described as the "good seeds. This point is now clearly demonstrated; thus, it is said that [the teaching] definitively reveals [the truth].

Below, the intention of the repeated objections is restated to refute what others have determined. [The categories are: the Great Determination, the Small Determination, the Determination of Essence, and the Determination of Ritual.

Since our school does not rely on the sutras for its finality, this is a wild determination and not the true ritual of the treatises. Our Patriarchs established the Perfect School precisely to support and complete [the teachings].
Because this school’s meaning is partially shared [with other teachings], it establishes the three clusters. What is the "superior resolution of emptiness and existence"?

This refers to manifesting the function of perfect fusion to aid conditions. When it is said that apart from these two sutras there is no such meaning elsewhere, it is precisely to demonstrate the basis of the Perfect School;
it clarifies that one employs the Great to receive the Small, rather than employing the Small to receive the Great, Small, and Great in their mutual fusion.

It is solely by means of two sutras—the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Lotus Sūtra), which reveals that śrāvakas attain Buddhahood, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, which supports the Lesser Vehicle while discussing the eternal—that [the true nature of precepts is revealed].
This is because the karma of prohibitions and observances arises from the poison of the mind; although the *Caturvargika-vinaya* prohibits such acts, it does not exhaust their root.

Therefore, in accordance with the intent of these two sutras to achieve perfect integration, a distinct school was established to broaden the study of the precepts, exhausting both principle and nature, and culminating in the reception of the Threefold Pure Precepts.

In the end, you have returned home; this is not according to the Sūtras, where the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations) for receiving the precepts requires a large assembly.

The meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*) as being "partially pervasive" (*fentong*) has been explained as before. Because you do not understand this, you falsely divide it into two meanings. Due to this ignorance, you stubbornly insist that the Great [Vehicle] is restricted to the Perfect, while claiming the Perfect is not limited to the Great.
You say that what is called "Great" is not necessarily Perfect, and therefore the Master of Records (Jizang), fearing precisely that one might be deluded by this, specifically extended his inquiry.

Answer: Your further twisting of the meaning only increases your deception. Within the *Ji* (Record/Commentary), you yourself stated that it refers to the "white-four-part" (*baisi*) Śrāvaka precepts;
why then do you steal the two characters "small" (*xiao*) and "great" (*da*) to mislead people?

You fail to recognize that "the small is identical to the great" (*xiaojijie da*)—you do not understand that this "small" is identical to the "great" because its principle is perfect, such that its entire substance is the same as the great. This is precisely the meaning of "identical" (*ji*) in the *Ji*.
It is said: "If one attains this essence," the single character "this" (此) corresponds to that "Great Precept" (大戒). Because you do not understand it, you instead cling to it as a basis for proof.

If one were to receive the Great Precept through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of one motion and three proclamations), it would perfectly accord with the meaning of the text; why then must it be resolved [only] in terms of receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*) of the highest grade?

This "highest grade" is precisely the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching]. As for what is called "resolving" (*jie*), it clarifies the meaning of receiving the full ordination of the highest grade in its perfect sense. You say that it has not yet...

If one argues that "roundness" depends on being determined by the square—that is, if the formal reception of the substance [of the precepts] through the arousal of the resolve (*cittotpāda*) is already complete, yet it only becomes "perfectly round" (*parimaṇḍala*) upon the subsequent practice—what logic is there for this?

If you claim that the subsequent roundness determines the prior establishment of the dharma so as to constitute a "perfectly round reception," then the sequence of the Patriarchal practice would be disrupted.

The proper ritual order is as follows: first, the arrangement of the conditions; second, the arousal of the resolve toward the objective sphere; third, the reception of the precepts based on that resolve; and finally, the demonstration of the substance. From beginning to end, this is a single, continuous process.

The *Guanshu* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) establishes the principle that the prior [stages] are subsumed by the subsequent; how could this be the same as establishing the "perfect decision" (*yuanjue*) within the "Chapter on Clarifying the Substance" (*mingti zhang*) at the very end?

What kind of argument is this?
